title: Powerful 7.3-Magnitude Earthquake Strikes Southern Mexico, Triggering Tsunami Warning

body:
Key Takeaways
  • A 7.3-magnitude earthquake struck Chiapas, Mexico, triggering a tsunami warning.
  • Tsunami waves could reach up to 1 meter along Mexican and Guatemalan coasts.
  • Aftershocks between magnitudes 5 and 6 were felt across the region.
  • The quake follows recent devastating earthquakes in Venezuela, raising regional fears.
  • Indians in affected areas are advised to stay alert and follow safety instructions.

A powerful magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck near the coast of Mexico's southernmost state of Chiapas on Friday morning, triggering a tsunami warning and sending tremors rippling through neighbouring Guatemala and El Salvador. Authorities reported no immediate casualties, but the quake rattled nerves across a region still reeling from the devastating twin earthquakes that hit Venezuela last month.

What Happened

The earthquake hit at approximately 7:48 a.m. local time at a depth of 15.2 kilometres, with its epicentre about 48 kilometres southwest of the town of Aquiles Serdán in Chiapas, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS). The USGS initially recorded the quake at magnitude 7.4 before revising it down to 7.3.

The U.S. Tsunami Warning System immediately issued an alert, warning that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along coasts within 300 kilometres of the epicentre. Waves could reach between 0.3 and 1 metre above tide level along parts of the Mexican and Guatemalan coasts, the agency said.

Mexico's Secretary of the Navy, Raymundo Morales, sought to calm fears during a government press conference. "There is no problem, no serious maritime impact," he said. "We only expect some beaches to see a rise in water level of up to half a metre due to the tsunami effect."

Regional Impact

In Guatemala City, the earthquake shook buildings and prompted panicked residents to flee onto the streets. "I got really scared and it reminded me of the recent earthquake in Venezuela. So I ran out and went down the stairs because I live on the eighth floor. The shaking wouldn't stop," Alexander Valdez, a 29-year-old accountant, told Reuters.

A series of aftershocks, including some registering between magnitudes 5 and 6, were felt across Mexico, Guatemala, and El Salvador. Local media in Guatemala showed footage of staff evacuating government buildings as security protocols were activated. The governor of the neighbouring Mexican state of Oaxaca confirmed tremors were felt in the state capital, Oaxaca de Juárez.

Regional Impact Overview
›Buildings shook in Guatemala City, causing panic.
›Residents evacuated government buildings in Guatemala.
›Tremors felt in Oaxaca de Juárez, Mexico.
›Aftershocks registered between magnitudes 5 and 6.

Venezuela's Shadow

The earthquake comes just three weeks after Venezuela was struck by devastating twin quakes on June 24 — magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 tremors that hit within less than a minute of each other, toppling buildings in Caracas and killing more than 4,900 people. The disaster has left Latin America on edge, and residents in Guatemala openly referenced the Venezuela catastrophe as they fled their homes on Friday.

Diaspora Watch

Venezuela's Recent Quakes
›Venezuela experienced twin quakes on June 24.
›Quakes were magnitude 7.2 and 7.5.
›Over 4,900 fatalities reported in Venezuela.
›Recent events heightened fears in neighboring countries.

Mexico and Guatemala are home to small but growing Indian diaspora communities, particularly in business and IT sectors. India's embassy in Mexico City has not yet issued a specific advisory, but Indians living in the affected states of Chiapas and Oaxaca are urged to stay alert and follow local safety instructions. Mexico sits atop three major tectonic plates, making it one of the world's most seismically active regions with a long history of devastating earthquakes.

The U.S. National Weather Service confirmed there was no tsunami threat to California or the broader Pacific coast.
